status: Two photographic trials for John to review
scope: The three illustrated steps of double digging. Steps 4 and 5 are text-only in the fixed page.

artwork.prompt:
Create a very wide horizontal photographic strip, a 3:1 triptych of THREE equal SQUARE photographs side by side edge-to-edge, fine plain white vertical seams only, no letters, numbers, labels, arrows or graphics. This is the actual illustration for three small steps on page 160 of a practical UK gardening book. Each square must work as an individual documentary photograph. A single fixed camera looking slightly down over the SAME small oblong patch in exactly the same Cornish back garden on the same softly overcast morning. NO people, hands, feet or body fragments anywhere. Make this look like a real gardener paused between actions for each photo.
First three references are the actual home. Ref 1 aerial maps locations only; refs 2-3 supply real material, viewpoint at ground and blue paint. Reconstruct a hypothetical grassy version: maintain the blue timber pent-roof shed at the left near the brown timber-clad building, the same weathered GREY HORIZONTAL-board fence stretching to the right across the back with shrubs above, the permanent pale individual square stepping stones across the back of our working patch. Keep the actual relative positions, fascias and roof angles. Turn all current growing beds and both greenhouses into continuous ordinary mown grass; no greenhouse, brick base, vegetable beds, planter, constructed edging or glass. Dig one new small bed into that lawn on the camera side of the stepping stones, leaving them free. Frame the ground as the main subject so a narrow but legible band across the top shows the recognisable blue shed and fence. Soft, clear daylight, restrained natural print colour, detailed moist-but-crumbly earth, no harsh exposure or fake bokeh. Looking obliquely from above close to the near end of the bed allows us to see down into the trench. Same lighting, position and crop across all frames. No model soil cutaway, no raised island, no timber border. Fourth reference is the THREE EXISTING BOOK DIAGRAMS, use ONLY to match the sequence of excavation and direction of movement. The trench goes ACROSS the short end of the oblong bed, full bed width, left to right like a single broad stair tread. Its width front-to-back and its depth are one spade blade (about 25cm), not a pit. The long direction of the future bed recedes away from us. Surrounding grass is plainly visible beyond both ends, remaining bed surface extends away. A small mound of removed first-trench topsoil sits on the grass to the left and stays intact in all three. 
LEFT — Opening. The first transverse trench has just been emptied, vertical freshly spade-cut face with thin grass roots at the surface, even firm EARTH floor visible below turf level. A real steel digging spade with wooden shaft and D-handle has been parked with its blade lightly sunk in/at the edge of the SIDE pile to the left. Small scattered dark compost on the undug strip beyond. This is a recently opened lawn.
CENTRE — Loosening underneath. SAME first trench in precisely the same spot, same saved soil. A four-tined long-handled digging fork angled slightly from vertical is planted right into the FLOOR of the open trench, lower than the turf. Show its steel head with tines part-engaged in the earth and a few dark compost crumbs among broken clods in the trench floor. No spade in this image. Keep trench open. No new pile of subsoil.
RIGHT — Move along the bed. ONE strip closer to camera has now been refilled with crumbly turned brown topsoil, grass buried. ONE newly exposed open transverse trench runs immediately BEHIND the refilled strip, one blade width farther away from camera. One spade with a small residue of soil is physically resting blade down on the refilled strip, shaft propped against the cut edge, or laid down on the near strip, NEVER hovering. The original soil pile is STILL to the left on grass. The filled strip in FRONT and new trench immediately BEHIND it must be visually unmistakable. Enough ordinary grass beyond. No other plots. Architectural details precisely repeated in all three, no extra buildings. Enough contrast between grass, blades, topsoil and the shadow of the cut that each stage reads at 43 mm printed width. Compose in three equal square panels across one wide 3:1 canvas, each panel filled with photographic scenery.

EDIT the first supplied photorealistic TRIPTYCH to make its companion for the same fixed book page. Add the ACTUAL male gardener shown in likeness photos 2, 3 and 4 demonstrating each action, once per panel. Preserve the same rural Cornish suburban rear garden geography, blue shed, timber-clad wall, weathered grey fence, slab path, hypothetical mown lawn and absence of all greenhouses and planters. Photo 1 controls all of the scenery, camera angle, strip positions, scale and distances; photos 2-4 supply the one real person's likeness, build and clothes ONLY, NOT their scenery; fifth image is the approved original instructional diagram ONLY. Very wide horizontal 3:1 strip, three equal square photographic panels separated by narrow white seams as in the first image, NO lettering, labels, borders, graphic diagrams or arrows. Close documentary garden photography in bright soft overcast daylight, no theatrical light. Keep essentially the same camera and soil framing for the three panels and for the unpeopled strip. The person on the right side of each image leans naturally into frame from the side of the patch, face seen in a readable three-quarter profile looking down at work, balding, short greying hair round the sides, short salt-and-pepper beard and moustache, the real Hackriculture gardener in the reference photos, relaxed blue/grey/red faded plaid overshirt sleeves rolled over a dark navy T-shirt, ordinary worn blue jeans and practical brown work boots. Keep his head in frame and tool blade visible at every stage; his face only a modest part of the image. Knees flexed, natural gardening posture, physically plausible hands, fingers, elbows, boots on firm untouched turf at the edge. Avoid portraiture or eye contact with camera. Put him to the right, leaving shed, left-side reserved soil heap and front face of actual trench easily visible. A man of normal scale using a normal adult spade, don't dwarf him. He can lean in low, adjust crop only the minimum necessary.
LEFT: he is just finishing opening the first single-spade-depth full-bed-width transverse trench across the near end. Show him tipping a modest spadeful of topsoil onto the SAVED pile immediately to LEFT of the trench. If easier he can work from near LEFT edge in just this panel. Already most of the trench is empty, simple flat bottom. Both hands on ONE real digging spade, one near the D grip, one partway down shaft. Show turf on the far side of the first cut.
MIDDLE: the SAME open first trench and same soil pile to left. He stands on undug turf at right, leaning into a long handled standard four-tined garden fork only, working the lower earth IN PLACE. Fork shoulder visibly down within the excavation with steel tines partly inserted into its FLOOR, flex and twist a little with broken clods, without lifting a forkful up. Keep the deep crosswise trench and engagement visible, no soil deposited on the grass and no extra tools.
RIGHT: preparing NEXT trench one strip farther from camera. There is one band of freshly returned crumbly soil right at the near end and immediately BEHIND it a single open transverse gap before the remaining grass. He is tipping a modest load of soil forward from this new strip into the PREVIOUS trench in front of it (toward camera). Spade blade carrying brown earth just above near strip, its handle visibly attached to his hands and dirt falling from blade onto that strip. Original reserved heap STILL at far left untouched. No tool duplications, no digging fork in this frame. Match the relative disposition of the strips shown in photo 1. Three exposures of ONE garden operation, composed so a reader sees a different operation in each even with photos printed at 43mm square.

checks: Three page copies at the original trim
Each page retained the original text, identical painting instructions and original illustration bounds
Original page rendered identically. At 144 dpi the only changed pixels on both trial pages are within the illustration rectangle.
review_notes: The lawn is a deliberate reconstruction. Shed details and the precise line of the paving are approximations. Check how deeply the middle fork appears engaged at print size and whether the third photo clearly shows topsoil moving into the previous trench. The original cutaway shows underground loosening directly.
